strengths: Provides a theoretical justification (Theorem 1) for replacing the standard Gaussian terminal distribution in diffusion models with a conditionally whitened Gaussian, giving a sufficient condition (KL divergence reduction) that motivates the design choices rather than being purely heuristic.

Proposes a unified and general framework (CW-Gen) that subsumes prior mean/variance-regressor approaches (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) as special cases and can be seamlessly integrated as a plug-in module into diverse existing diffusion and flow-matching backbones.

The Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE) jointly models the conditional mean and sliding-window covariance with a Cholesky-based PSD parameterization and an eigenvalue regularization term, directly linked to the theoretical sufficient condition, which is a reasonably principled design.
Extends the whitening idea beyond diffusion (CW-Diff) to flow matching (CW-Flow), improving computational efficiency by avoiding explicit matrix inversion at each step.

Reasonably broad empirical evaluation: 5 datasets, 6 base generative models (both diffusion and flow-based), 4 main metrics plus 2 additional point-forecast metrics, 10 random seeds with standard deviations reported, and win-rate summaries showing fairly consistent improvement.
Qualitative illustrations (Figure 2) support the claim that CW-Gen mitigates distribution shift and produces tighter, more accurate uncertainty bands compared to non-whitened counterparts.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 gives only a sufficient (not necessary) condition and is stated as an inequality that is difficult to interpret in practice; there is no empirical verification that the condition actually holds for the trained JMCE estimators on the real datasets, weakening the claimed link between theory and observed empirical gains.

The comparison between CW-Gen and baseline prior-informed methods (TMDM, NsDiff) is somewhat unfair/confounded since CW-Gen uses a more powerful Non-stationary Transformer backbone for JMCE, whereas baselines use their original (often simpler) regressors; it's unclear how much of the gain is due to the whitening idea versus the stronger estimator architecture.

Win-rate reporting (e.g., 'CW-Gen outperforms in 22/24 cases') aggregates across metrics/models/datasets without statistical significance testing, and given the noticeable overlap in reported standard deviations (e.g., TMDM/NSDiff CRPS in Table 2), some improvements may not be statistically significant.

Only one dataset (ETTh1) is shown in the main text with full result tables; results for ETTh2, ILI, Weather, and Solar Energy are deferred to tables 3-6 not shown in the excerpt, making it hard to fully assess consistency of gains, especially on higher-dimensional data (Solar Energy has notably lower win rate at 79%).

The computational overhead of training JMCE (an additional non-autoregressive Transformer model) and its cost during inference is not clearly quantified or compared against baseline runtime/parameter counts, despite claiming CW-Flow's efficiency advantage over CW-Diff.

The paper doesn't sufficiently discuss failure cases or limitations of the method, e.g., when covariance estimation is poor or in very high-dimensional settings where O(d^3) eigendecomposition (for CW-Diff) could become a bottleneck.

The relationship and comparative advantage of CW-Gen over NsDiff (which also models heteroscedasticity via mean/variance regressors) is asserted qualitatively but not tightly established: Theorem 2 (comparing against TMDM/NsDiff) is relegated entirely to the appendix and not discussed in the main text, leaving the core novelty argument against the closest baseline under-supported in the main paper.

Notational density and heavy reliance on appendices (proofs, algorithms, extra results) makes the main paper harder to verify standalone; several key implementation details (e.g., choice of window size, architecture specifics of JMCE) are deferred, limiting reproducibility from the main text alone.

strengths: Provides a principled theoretical foundation (Theorem 1 and 2) establishing sufficient conditions under which replacing the standard Gaussian terminal distribution of diffusion models with a conditionally whitened one improves KL divergence to the true conditional distribution, with rigorous, self-contained proofs.

Unifies existing prior-informed diffusion approaches (CARD, TMDM, NsDiff) as special cases of the proposed CW-Gen framework, and clearly articulates their specific limitations (e.g., ignoring covariance, complicated reverse process) that CW-Gen addresses.

Proposes a well-motivated Joint Mean-Covariance Estimator (JMCE) using Cholesky parameterization and an explicit eigenvalue regularization term directly derived from the theoretical sufficient condition, which is a nice link between theory and method design.

Extensive empirical evaluation across 6 generative backbones (5 diffusion models + 1 flow matching) and 5 real-world datasets of varying dimensionality/domain, using multiple complementary metrics (CRPS, QICE, ProbCorr, Conditional FID, ProbMSE/MAE), showing fairly consistent improvements.

Thorough ablation studies (hyperparameters wEigen/λmin, backbone choice, sliding window length, joint vs separate mean/covariance training, individual prior components) that support the design choices and increase confidence in the empirical claims.

Addresses practical computational concerns via an accelerated whitening scheme (avoiding eigen-decomposition) and an end-to-end training variant, along with reported wall-clock training times across datasets.
Includes comparisons against additional non-diffusion/flow prior-informed baselines (DSPD, TsFlow) to contextualize the contribution relative to broader literature.
weaknesses: The theoretical sufficient conditions (Theorem 1, Eq. 3; Theorem 2, Eq. 9) are never empirically verified to actually hold in the experiments; the paper only shows JMCE achieves low estimation error, not that the conditions are satisfied in practice, leaving a gap between theory and demonstrated applicability.

Method incurs cubic computational complexity O(d^3) from eigen-decomposition for CW-Diff, which becomes a serious bottleneck on higher-dimensional datasets (e.g., Solar Energy training time balloons to ~24,000s for JMCE alone), and the benefits of CW-Gen are visibly weaker on this dataset (lower win rates, mixed ProbMSE results at 50%).
Reproducibility statement provides a code link placeholder that is blank/missing, undermining the reproducibility claim despite detailed algorithmic pseudocode in the appendix.

Some individual results are inconsistent or unfavorable for CW-Gen (e.g., SSSD on Weather has worse CRPS under CW; ILI QICE win rate is only 33%), and the paper does not perform statistical significance testing across seeds despite reporting standard deviations.

The empirical comparison is restricted almost entirely to diffusion/flow-matching baselines; other established probabilistic forecasting approaches (e.g., normalizing flows, GP-copula models, deep AR-based probabilistic methods) are not compared, limiting the demonstrated positioning relative to the broader probabilistic forecasting literature.

Sensitivity to the sliding-window covariance size appears non-trivial on smaller datasets (ILI), suggesting the method's practical robustness may be dataset-dependent and require careful tuning that isn't fully characterized.

The paper is notation-heavy and dense, with many interacting components (JMCE loss terms, Cholesky whitening operations, multiple hyperparameters), which may hinder accessibility and independent reimplementation despite the provided algorithms.
